questions.stemHtml: A 7-year-old child presents with fever, erythematous rash, and bone pain. X-ray of the skull shows multiple lytic lesions. Skin biopsy shows prominent nuclear grooves with eosinophils as in the image below. Immunohistochemistry for S100, CD1a is also shown in the images below. What would be the diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
The above clinical scenario along with the histopathological image showing Langerhans cells with folded nuclei (image A), CD1a (image B), and positive S100 (image C), is suggestive of Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH).

LCH occurs due to the proliferation of a special type of immature dendritic cells, called Langerhans cells. Their normal function is to present antigens. The most common mutation is the BRAFV600E gain-of-function mutation.

It is characterized by single or multiple osteolytic bone lesions and can also infiltrate nearly every organ, like the skin (of the scalp), lungs, liver, spleen, bone marrow, or the central nervous system. 

LCH can present as the following clinical entities:

  • Multifocal multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis (Letterer-Siwe disease) - mostly seen in infants
  • Unifocal and multifocal unisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis (eosinophilic granuloma) - The combination of bone defects, diabetes insipidus, and exophthalmos is called the Hand-Schüller-Christian triad - mostly seen in younger children
  • Pulmonary LCH - mostly seen in adults

Clinical features include pain and swelling in the affected area. When calvarium is affected, it results in otitis media and mastoiditis. Spinal involvement results in compression fractures and neurological involvement. Vertebral involvement results in a rapid flattening of the vertebral body (vertebra plana).

Histopathologically, Langerhans cells have a single large nucleus with a characteristic folded or grooved nucleus (coffee-bean appearance) with small inconspicuous nucleoli. Birbeck granules are seen in the cytoplasm. The tumor cells specifically express HLA-DR, S-100, and CD1a and langerin (CD207) markers.

The image below shows a histopathological image of Langerhans cells with folded nuclei.



The presence of Birbeck granules in the cytoplasm is a characteristic finding of Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) on electron microscopy.

Birbeck granules have a dilated terminal end producing a tennis racket–like appearance. It contains the protein langerin (CD207). It is seen on electron microscopy. The image below shows Birbeck granules on electron microscopy seen in LCH.



The below image shows lytic lesion of skull seen in LCH.



Option A: Rosai-Dorfman syndrome is otherwise called sinus histiocytosis with massive lymphadenopathy. Rosai-Dorfman disease is not a histiocytic neoplasm. It is an idiopathic disease characterized by Painless lymphadenopathy, usually of cervical nodes. The disorder predominantly affects children, adolescents, and young adults. It may present with nonspecific symptoms and management mostly involves observation rather than specific treatment.  

Option B: Kimura disease is s a chronic inflammatory disorder of unknown etiology that most commonly presents as painless lymphadenopathy.

Option D: Juvenile xanthogranuloma is a non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis occurring in early infancy and childhood. It presents as reddish-brown papular lesions, which evolve to become orange. The lesions are most frequently seen in the face, scalp, and upper torso. They may be single or multiple lesions. Single lesions are the most common. The characteristic multinucleated giant cell, Touton cell is observed in 85% of juvenile xanthogranulomas.

questions.stem: Match the following cell types with their associated malignancy.
questions.solutionHtml:
The correct matches are as follows:

1. Popcorn cell b. Lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin's lymphoma
2. Faggot cell a. Acute promyelocytic leukemia
3. Cerebriform nuclei d. Sezary syndrome
4. Starry sky c. Burkitt lymphoma

 

Popcorn cell is a lymphohistiocytic (L&H) variant of Reed Steenberg (RS) cells that are characteristic of lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma. It has a delicate multilobed, puffy nucleus resembling popped corn. The image below shows a popcorn cell seen in lymphocytic predominant Hodgkin's lymphoma.



Multiple Auer rods clustered together within a single cell resembling a bundle of sticks are known as faggot cells and are highly suggestive of acute promyelocytic leukemia. Histopathology from bone marrow aspirate reveals numerous Auer rods (needle-like azurophilic granules) in the cytoplasm of the promyelocytes. Faggot cells are shown below.



Sézary-Lutzner cells - cells with cerebriform nuclei (infolded/hyper-convoluted nuclear membrane).

The histological hallmark of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides type) is the presence of Sezary-Lutzner cells, which form band-like aggregates within the superficial dermis and invade the epidermis as single cells and small clusters called Pautrier microabscess (marked by arrow). These cells have markedly infolded nuclear membranes giving them a cerebriform contour as seen below.



Microscopy in Burkitt lymphoma shows a characteristic starry sky pattern. The neoplastic cells are homogeneous, medium-sized B cells with frequent mitotic figures and reactive macrophages scattered through the tumor, with their pale cytoplasm in a background of blue-staining tumor cells giving the tumor a so-called "starry sky" appearance.

The image given below shows a starry sky pattern seen in Burkitt lymphoma.

questions.stem: Hereditary angioedema is due to a defect in which of the proteins mentioned below?
questions.solutionHtml:
Hereditary angioedema is an autosomal dominant condition characterized by a deficiency of C1 esterase inhibitors. C1 esterase inhibitors usually target proteases like C1r and C1s, factor XII and the kallikrein system. Therefore, their deficiency leads to unregulated activation of kallikrein, leading to increased bradykinin.

Clinical features include swelling of the skin and mucosal surfaces, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, which may be aggravated after minor trauma or emotional stress. The condition can be treated by giving C1 inhibitor concentrates from human plasma. 

The main inflammatory mediator responsible for these symptoms is bradykinin. Bradykinin is an inflammatory mediator formed by the cleavage of kininogen, in the presence of the enzyme kallikrein. Bradykinin has the following effects:

  • Increases the vascular permeability
  • Causes contraction of smooth muscle
  • Dilates the blood vessel 
  • Mediates pain

Other options:

Options B and C: Decay-accelerating factor (DAF) and CD59 are two proteins that are linked by a glycophosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor to the plasma membrane. DAF prevents the formation of C3 convertases and CD59 inhibits the formation of the MAC. An acquired deficiency of the enzyme that creates GPI anchors leads to a deficiency of these regulators and excessive complement activation and lysis of red cells resulting in Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria(PNH).

During inflammation, C5a (Option D), C3a, and C4a, which are all cleavage products of their corresponding complement components, stimulate mast cells to release histamine. They have effects similar to those of mast cell mediators involved in anaphylactic reactions and therefore, are called anaphylatoxins. C5a is also chemotactic for neutrophils, monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils. Additionally, it activates the lipooxygenase pathway of arachidonic acid metabolism in neutrophils and monocytes, resulting in the further release of inflammatory mediators.





Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10e, Page no 85 table 3.5, 91, 92, 242

questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old woman presents with fatigue. Investigations revealed the following: Hb, 5 gm %; MCH, 24; low MCV; leukocytes, 11,000/uL, and platelets, 5 lakhs. The peripheral smear is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
The given scenario of a 35 year old woman, her iron profile and peripheral smear showing microcytic hypochromic anemia are suggestive of iron-deficiency anemia (IDA).

IDA is an example of microcytic hypochromic anemia. The causes of IDA can be inadequate diet, impaired reabsorption, increased requirement and increased blood loss.

The manifestations of IDA depend upon the underlying cause. In general, IDA presents with koilonychia, alopecia, atrophic changes in the tongue, gastric mucosa, malabsorbtion and pica (craving for consumption of non-edible materials)

Peripheral smears show small and pale red cells typically described as microcytic (reduced MCV) and hypochromic (enlarged zone of central pallor). Poikilocytosis can be seen in the form of elongated red cells, known as pencil cells. Target cells can be found in cases of severe IDA.

Diagnosis is mainly by laboratory studies. The typical findings are:

  • Low hemoglobin and hematocrit
  • Low serum iron and ferretin
  • Increased Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC)
  • Hepcidin is low (decreased stores of iron inhibit hepcidin synthesis)

IDA is treated by giving oral and parenteral preparations if iron or packed cell transfusion depending upon the severity of the anemia.

Option A: Megaloblastic anemia is defined by a high MCV

Option C: Thalassemia presents much earlier in infancy, with reduced MCV and a normal/increased RBC count

Option D: Essential thrombocytosis is characterized by isolated rise in platelet count (>450,000) along with normal hemoglobin, hematocrit and iron stores.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true about interleukin-12?
questions.solutionHtml:
The true statements are that interleukin-12 (IL-12) is produced by macrophages and increases the production of interferon-γ (IFN-γ).

IL-12 is produced by dendritic cells and macrophages. Its principle actions are to promote the production of IFN-γ, which drives TH1-type responses and further stimulates macrophage activation. It also promotes the differentiation of CD4+ T-cells to Th1 cells.

questions.stem: A chronic smoker presents to the clinic with shortness of breath. A mass is noted at the lower lobe periphery of the lung. A diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma is made. The biopsy will be positive for:
questions.solutionHtml:
The biopsy of adenocarcinoma of the lung will be positive for thyroid transcription factor-1 (TTF-1) and napsin A.

Adenocarcinoma is an invasive malignant epithelial tumor with glandular differentiation or mucin production by the tumor cells. It is associated with tobacco smoking, but less so than other histologic subtypes. It is the most common subtype in non-smokers and is associated with the loss of function of EGFR, ALK, ROS1, MET or RET genes.

The majority express TTF-1, which is a protein required for normal lung development. Napsin A is a new marker and is more sensitive and specific than TTF-1 in the diagnosis of adenocarcinoma.

Adenocarcinomas grow in various patterns: acinar, lepidic, papillary, micropapillary, and solid. The lesions are small and are usually located in the periphery.  At the periphery of the tumor there is often a lepidic pattern of spread, in which the tumor cells “crawl” along normal-appearing alveolar septa. 

Clinical features usually have an insidious onset. The incidence is usually at age 50 or more. The major presenting complaints are cough, weight loss, chest pain, and dyspnea.    

Other options:

Option B: p40, along with p63 is a marker for squamous cell carcinoma of the lung.

Option D: Chromogranin is a marker for small cell carcinoma of the lung.

questions.stemHtml: The following image shows an instrument used to estimate hemoglobin levels. What does it measure?
questions.solutionHtml:
The instrument in the image is Sahli's hemoglobinometer and is used to measure acid hematin levels of a given blood sample. 

In Sahli's method, oxyhemoglobin is converted to acid hematin with the action of dilute hydrochloric acid (N/10 HCl). The brown color of the acid hematin is matched to its intensity with a standard brown glass comparator in a visual colorimeter called Sahli’s colorimeter.

Sahli's method is a simple bedside test and is cost-effective. However, it has some disadvantages which include visual errors, inability to measure other forms of hemoglobin, fading of the comparator over time, and the color of acid hematin fading quickly.





Online Resource, Practical Pathology by Harsh Mohan (3rd ed); Pages 192, 193

questions.stem: Iron in tissues is stained by:
questions.solutionHtml:
Perl's Prussian blue stain is used in histopathological studies to detect the presence of iron in the specimen. Iron is stained blue with this stain.

It is used in hereditary hemochromatosis to stain liver tissue, which shows hepatocellular iron. It also stains the iron-laden mitochondria of ring sideroblasts seen in lead toxicity and myelodysplastic syndrome

The following image shows the blue staining of iron (in the form of hemosiderin) deposited in hepatocytes:



Other options:

Option A: Masson's trichrome stain is used to stain collagen.

Option C: PAS stain (Periodic acid Schiff stain) is used for the detection of glycogen in tissues such as the liver, skeletal muscle, etc., and also in tumor cells. 

Option D: Fite-Faraco stain has been used in cases of leprosy for staining Mycobacterium leprae. It can also be used to stain Nocardia.

questions.stemHtml: A woman presents with lesions on the inner thighs and peri-anal region. They are nodular, 4-6 mm in size, and appear pale. The histopathological image shows multiple intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies consistent with Henderson-Patterson bodies. The diagnosis is:
questions.solutionHtml:
The diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario and the histological image is molluscum contagiosum, which shows intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies, called Henderson–Patterson bodies or molluscum bodies.

Infection is usually spread by direct contact, particularly among children and young adults. Multiple lesions occur on the skin and mucous membranes, with a predilection for the trunk and anogenital areas. Individual lesions are firm, pruritic, pink to skin-colored umbilicated papules. A curd-like material can be expressed from the central umbilication.

Smearing this material onto a glass slide followed by Giemsa staining shows diagnostic molluscum bodies, which are ellipsoid, homogeneous, cytoplasmic inclusion bodies that are found in the cells of the stratum granulosum and the stratum corneum and are up to 35 μm in size.

The image below shows umbilicated papules of molluscum contagiosum. 

 



Other options: 

Option A: Trichodysplasia spinulosa is a condition characterized by painless erythematous papules on the face with folliculocentric keratin spines. It is caused by trichodysplasia spinulosa-associated polyomavirus. Histologic features are keratin plugging, abundant dystrophic and cornfield inner root sheath epithelium, and numerous, large eosinophilic trichohyalin granules.

Option B: Koilocytes are characteristically seen in HPV infections, such as condylomata acuminata. Koilocytes are lining cells which have perinuclear cytoplasmic vacuolization.

Option D: Donovan bodies are seen in donovanosis, caused by Klebsiella granulomatis. Donovan bodies are minute, encapsulated coccobacilli in macrophages, which can be demonstrated in Giemsa-stained smears of the exudate.

questions.stem: Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction is caused by all of the following cytokines except:
questions.solutionHtml:
INF-γ is not involved in Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction (JHR).

JHR is a condition that occurs in patients infected by spirochetes who undergo antibiotic treatment. The reaction occurs within 24 hours of antibiotic treatment. Clinical features are fever, chills, nausea and vomiting, tachycardia, hypotension, flushing, myalgia, and exacerbation of skin lesions.

Syphilis is the leading spirochetal infection associated with JHR. Other infections are Lyme disease, louse-borne relapsing fever, leptospirosis, and tick-borne relapsing fever. Antibiotics that have been most associated are penicillins, tetracyclines, and erythromycin.

Mild reactions are self-limiting and often resolve spontaneously within 24 hours. Prevention of the JHR is by giving TNF-alpha antibodies and in some cases steroids.





Online Resource, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557820/#:~:text=Jarisch%20Herxheimer%20reaction%20(JHR)%20is,Lyme%20disease%2C%20and%20relapsing%20fever.
